metadata.title: How Many Years of Pay Buy a Home?
metadata.section: Section D: Demographics, Real Estate & Urban Drift
metadata.data_notes: Median home value divided by median household income (Census ACS, yearly). 2020 was not published, so 2019-2021 is a straight-line fill. Los Angeles changed its metro code in 2013; both codes are joined.

events.label: Housing bubble peak: New York at 7.7 years of income
Post-crash low: San Francisco at 7.4 years
Austin peaks at 5.2 years of income

explanation.summary: How many years of a typical household's income would it take to pay for a typical home? This chart answers that for ten large metro areas, with the US average as a line. A ratio of 3 is often called affordable. Los Angeles and San Francisco have stayed far above that for twenty years, while Austin has climbed the fastest. Pittsburgh is still close to 3.
explanation.methodology: Median home value (ACS table B25077) divided by median household income (B19013) for each metro area and for the whole US, from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey 1-year estimates, 2005-2024. Home values are reported by owners. 2020 1-year data was not released, so 2019-2021 is a straight line. Los Angeles changed its metro code in 2013 (31100 to 31080); both are joined.

key_findings.title: 2005: Bubble-Era Prices
key_findings.description: A San Francisco home cost 10.0 years of income and a New York home 7.5 years. Austin (3.2) and Chicago (4.3) were far cheaper.
key_findings.significance: Coastal homes were already out of reach for typical earners before the crash.

key_findings.title: 2012: After the Crash
key_findings.description: After the crash, San Francisco fell to 7.4 years, its lowest. Chicago fell to 3.5 years and kept falling, to 3.4 years in 2019. Prices fell faster than incomes.
key_findings.significance: The crash made homes more affordable, but credit was hard to get.

key_findings.title: 2022: Austin's Boom
key_findings.description: Austin rose to 5.2 years of income, up from 3.1 in 2006, as tech companies and remote workers moved in. In 2024 the ratios were San Francisco 8.4, New York 6.5, Austin 4.8 and Chicago 3.7.
key_findings.significance: Austin moved from a cheap city to an expensive one in about ten years.
